title: Identifiability-Guided Composite Load Modeling of AI Data Centers
summary: The rapid growth of AI data centers introduces large, workload-dependent loads whose protection and reconnection behavior can affect power-system transient stability. Calibrating dynamic models of such loads is challenging because treating all associated elements as freely estimable may lead to weakly identified or physically confounded parameterizations. This paper proposes an identifiability-guided calibration framework for a composite load model with separate IT, cooling, and auxiliary branches. A nuisance-projected Fisher-information criterion characterizes the local identifiability of the cooling-motor composition, while a workload non-equivalence result shows that voltage-only recalibration cannot reproduce workload-dependent responses. Guided by these results, a grey-box estimator trained with branch-level supervision learns the workload-to-power relation and the cooling composition, while retaining a prescribed UPS protection law and an externally anchored reconnect-ramp duration. The learned workload relation is then distilled into a closed form for transient-stability simulation. Evaluation using 300,000 MIT Supercloud GPU power-utilization samples and 12,600 IEEE 39-bus fault scenarios yields an aggregate active-power $R^2$ of 0.948, compared with 0.856 for an LSTM baseline. Removing branch-level supervision preserves relatively high aggregate accuracy but substantially degrades cooling-component recovery. Under unseen deep voltage sags, the proposed model achieves a transient $R^2$ of 0.750, compared with 0.033 for the LSTM. Closed-loop simulations further show that cooling composition and protection behavior can affect retained-load states and voltage responses near protection thresholds.

title: Physical AI: A Survey of Models, Learning, Systems, and Open Challenges
summary: Physical AI aims to enable intelligent systems to perceive, reason, act, and learn through interaction with the physical world. Unlike purely digital intelligence, physical agents must operate under partial observability, uncertain dynamics, embodiment constraints, and real-time requirements, while their actions continuously reshape the environment and subsequent observations. Recent advances in foundation models and robot learning have expanded the capabilities of physical agents, yet achieving reliable autonomy requires more than improvements in individual models. This survey presents a comprehensive, system-level review of Physical AI, organized around the closed-loop process of physical interaction. We examine the foundations and recent developments in task representations and memory, predictive and action-generating models, data and learning methods, embodiment and control, computing systems, evaluation, and safety. Beyond reviewing individual advances, we investigate how these components interact and collectively shape the capabilities and limitations of Physical AI systems. Building on this integrated perspective, we identify fundamental challenges in generalization, resource-efficient learning and execution, reliable state tracking, safety, recovery, and continual adaptation. We argue that advancing Physical AI requires moving beyond isolated model performance toward integrated systems capable of robust, efficient, safe, and autonomous physical interaction under changing real-world conditions.

title: Joint Subcarrier and Power Allocation for Localization-Oriented Multi-Carrier Underwater ISAC Systems
summary: Multi-carrier underwater integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) realizes concurrent acoustic communication and localization, yet the frequency selectivity of the acoustic channel creates uneven positioning capabilities across subcarriers. This paper proposes a localization-oriented subcarrier and power allocation scheme for multi-anchor underwater ISAC systems. We build a unified orthogonal subcarrier multiplexing framework and derive closed-form Cramer-Rao bounds (CRBs) under frequency-selective channels with colored noise. We derive a subcarrier-level localization information contribution from the time of arrival Fisher information, which enables localization-oriented resource allocation. We derive several theoretical properties regarding the distance and frequency dependence of the localization information metric, and establish a distance-frequency matching principle. These results provide a theoretical foundation for localization-oriented resource allocation and guide the design of a low-complexity greedy algorithm that improves positioning accuracy. Specifically, the algorithm iteratively allocates subcarriers to minimize the residual positioning-error objective, thereby improving positioning accuracy while satisfying communication quality-of-service (QoS) constraints. Simulations verify that our method yields much lower positioning error bound than uniform, random and high-frequency-first subcarrier allocation in symmetric or asymmetric topologies while guaranteeing communication QoS, achieving superior communication-localization tradeoffs.

title: Topological entropy of nonlinear time-varying systems
summary: We study the topological entropy of nonlinear time-varying systems. We establish conditions under which entropy is independent of the initial time and derive two general upper bounds based on the matrix measure of the system Jacobian and the spectral abscissa of a Metzler comparison matrix, respectively. A general lower bound is also obtained using the trace of the Jacobian. For interconnected systems, we first derive an upper bound using the matrix measure of an interconnection matrix constructed from the Jacobian blocks. We then establish a new upper bound based on the spectral abscissa of a Metzler comparison matrix, incorporating the interconnection structure through subsystem-wise trajectory-separation analysis. This bound also recovers the two general upper bounds as special cases. All bounds depend on asymptotic properties of the Jacobian over reachable sets or their convex hulls. Simple examples show that either general upper bound may be tighter, while a time-varying Lorenz system illustrates the effects of norm selection and subsystem decomposition.

title: When is cumulative dose response monotonic? Analysis of incoherent feedforward motifs
comments: A shorter version of this work is to appear in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control
summary: We study the monotonicity of the cumulative dose response (cDR) for a class of incoherent feedforward motifs (IFFM) systems with linear intermediate dynamics and nonlinear output dynamics. While the instantaneous dose response (DR) may be nonmonotone with respect to the input, the cDR can still be monotone. To analyze this phenomenon, we derive an integral representation of the sensitivity of cDR with respect to the input and establish general sufficient conditions for both monotonicity and nonmonotonicity. These results reduce the problem to verifying qualitative sign properties along system trajectories. The structural conditions identify eight canonical IFFM models, four of which are analyzed in detail within the proposed framework. In particular, IFFM1 and IFFM3 exhibit monotone cDR despite potentially nonmonotone DR, while IFFM2 is monotone already at the level of DR, which implies monotonicity of cDR. In contrast, IFFM4 exhibits nonmonotone cDR. Numerical simulations indicate that these properties persist beyond the structured initial conditions used in the analysis. Overall, our results provide a unified framework for understanding how system structure shapes monotonicity in cumulative input--output responses.
comment: A shorter version of this work is to appear in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control

title: Rate-Cost Tradeoffs in Nonlinear Control
summary: We study finite-horizon rate-cost tradeoffs for general stochastic control systems, including nonlinear systems. Under an average control cost constraint, we show that the minimum expected communication rate lies within an additive logarithmic gap above the normalized directed information minimized over causal control policies. This establishes directed information as the operationally relevant quantity governing rate-limited control, extending its previously established roles in causal source coding and linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control to general nonlinear control systems.

title: Virtual Speech Therapist: A Clinician-in-the-Loop AI Agent for Speech Therapy Planning
summary: This paper presents a proof of concept of the Virtual Speech Therapist (VST), an intelligent multi-agent based system designed to support stuttering assessment and individualized therapy planning through artificial intelligence (AI) driven workflows. VST integrates deep learning (DL) based stuttering detection fSD with large language model (LLM) based agentic system to assist clinicians in developing evidence informed therapy plans. The VST system begins with the acquisition and feature extraction of given speech samples, followed by the detection of stuttering types. Building on these speech driven information S, VST initiates an agentic reasoning process in which specialized LLM agents autonomously generate, critique, and iteratively refine individualized therapy plans P. A dedicated CriticAgent πca acts as a structured self-refinement mechanism, reviewing the generated therapy plans P and identifying areas for potential improvement in consistency, methodological soundness, and alignment with available evidence and professional guidelines. The resulting therapy plan P is presented then as a draft for clinician review. Clinician feedback can then be incorporated to produce a revised plan P, thereby maintaining a clinician-in-the-loop (CITL) paradigm. An initial evaluation, involving expert speech language pathologist (SLP) examines the clinical interpretability and feasibility of the generated therapy plans. Taken together, the results show the potential of VST to augment clinician-led therapy planning and provide a promising basis for future studies evaluating its integration into real world clinical settings. An interactive user interface for the proposed prototype is available online at: https://vocametrix.com/ai/stuttering-therapy-planning-agent, facilitating interactive stuttering assessment and stuttering therapy planning.

title: FracEvent: Event-Camera Simulation via Fractional-Relaxation Pixel Dynamics
comments: Accepted to WACV 2027. 25 pages including supplementary material
summary: Event cameras asynchronously report brightness changes with microsecond-level temporal resolution, but real event data remain difficult to collect at scale because specialized sensors, careful synchronization, and task-specific annotations are required. Event-camera simulation is therefore important to event-based vision tasks. Most practical simulators build on contrast-threshold event generation, some with additional filtering, stochastic noise, or calibrated sensor parameters. While effective, such formulations can simplify the temporal structure produced by a pixel's recent response history. We introduce FracEvent, a physics-inspired sensor-side simulator with compact fractional-relaxation voltage dynamics. Given a log-intensity trajectory, FracEvent combines fast and slow response modes, emits ON/OFF events by localizing threshold crossings on the continuous voltage trajectory, and updates the event reference while retaining the mode states. This retained state links residual response to later event timing. We evaluate FracEvent through direct event-stream comparison and downstream transfer on image reconstruction and optical flow estimation. Across multiple datasets, FracEvent achieves leading results on multiple metrics in both evaluations, showing its practical value for event-camera simulation. Project page: https://bonaparte233.github.io/FracEvent/
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 25 pages including supplementary material

title: Revisiting the Relation Between Language Model Perplexity and ASR Word Error Rate for Modern End-to-End Speech Recognition
summary: Language model (LM) perplexity (PPL) has historically been used as a proxy for automatic speech recognition (ASR) word error rate (WER), with prior work reporting an approximately linear relation in log-log space. Modern end-to-end ASR systems challenge this assumption because they already contain internal language modeling capacity, are often evaluated without external language models, and can now be combined with neural LMs and large language models (LLMs) through different recognition strategies. This paper revisits the relation between PPL and WER for modern ASR systems. We study whether external LMs still improve current end-to-end ASR systems, whether the PPL-WER relation remains linear in log-log space, how encoder context length affects this relation, and how LLM perplexities fit into the trend observed for standard neural LMs. We further investigate internal language modeling (ILM) in attention-based encoder-decoder systems and show that ILM subtraction changes the observed PPL-WER relation, indicating that the decoder's internal LM must be considered when interpreting the effect of external LM quality.

title: MIRA: A Modular Open-Source Micro-UAV for Indoor Research
summary: Indoor robotics research increasingly relies on micro-UAV platforms whose airframes, electronics, and control software are open to modification. Off-the-shelf platforms often lack the low-level access that such modifications require, while building a custom vehicle demands substantial engineering effort before the first flight test, leaving many laboratories working within constraints that limit the scope of their research. We present MIRA (Modular Indoor Research Architecture), an open-source micro-UAV for indoor research, built around a replicable 3D-printed PLA airframe with detachable arms and a containerized low-level software package that manages the companion-to-autopilot communication bridge via Micro XRCE-DDS. Designed as a white-box architecture, its core subsystems, including the companion computer, are individually replaceable without firmware refactoring, which supports local fabrication, crash-localized repair, and component substitution from existing laboratory inventory. We characterize MIRA through autonomous flights comprising takeoff, hovering, trajectory tracking, and landing within an optical motion-capture volume. The communication pipeline sustains a median companion-to-autopilot latency of 0.02 ms, with the external motion-capture link as the main remaining latency source, and time-domain analysis shows that structural vibration remains stable during dynamic maneuvers and below the reference level adopted in this work. All design files and software are released openly to support replication and extension by other laboratories.

title: Mode-Weighted Transport Certificates for State-Dependent Reflected Switching Diffusions
summary: State-dependent switching diffusions can contract in law even when individual modes are expansive. We establish a computable, constant-one contraction certificate on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and compact convex domains with normal reflection. The mode-weighted transport cost combines spatial separation with a discrete graph penalty and retains spatial dependence when the modes differ. A synchronous Brownian coupling and a maximal coupling of jump clocks in equal modes lead to separate equal- and unequal-mode generator inequalities. We give a complete regularization argument for the nonsmooth cost, including the drift and jump errors, the sign of reflection, and the limiting Itô-Dynkin calculation. A resolvent proof transfers contraction to probability-valued weak solutions of the no-flux Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov system, while an explicit Foster-Lyapunov condition ensures existence and uniqueness of an invariant law on the whole space. For fixed weight ordering and decay rate, certificate synthesis is a semi-infinite linear feasibility problem; on compact domains, a Lipschitz-buffered finite mesh provides a rigorous test. One-dimensional and planar examples illustrate the certificate and its numerical verification.

title: Repeated Binary Direct Collinear Impacts Under Incremental Contact Laws With Residual Indentation: A Hybrid Systems Formulation
summary: Incremental contact laws specify the normal contact force through a differential relation, possibly carrying an internal state, driven by the indentation and its rate. In some, the force is extinguished at a nonzero indentation, whether by plastic deformation or by an elastic aftereffect, so that a residual deformation remains at separation. Such laws sit uneasily within rigid body dynamics, which admits no deformation. The tension is tolerable when the indentation is small relative to the bodies, so that it may be carried constitutively rather than geometrically. Even then, the contact law alone does not determine the interaction of the bodies. Because force and indentation no longer vanish together, conditions for the commencement and termination of contact must be supplied separately. So must the fate of the deformation and internal state at separation, neither of which the equations of motion contain. This article formulates the repeated direct collinear impact of two convex bodies under external forces as a hybrid dynamical system. The contact interface is modeled as a massless element carrying the contact law and its state, coupled to the bodies through relative velocity and an interaction force dictated by the contact state. Consequently, all switching and resets are confined to the interface, leaving the geometry and the equations of motion of the bodies unaltered. The principal analytical properties of the resulting formulations are established, among them passivity and completeness; the branching of solutions at the onset and termination of contact is also examined. The framework is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

title: From Generative to Discriminative: Lightweight Adaptation of SpeechLLMs for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
comments: Under review at ACL Rolling Review (ARR)
summary: SpeechLLMs can recognise emotion by generating a label token, but this approach relies on the LLM's existing output representations. We compare this generative approach with a discriminative alternative that uses a linear classification head on top of the LLM's hidden states. Because most multimodal emotion recognition studies evaluate with ground-truth transcripts, whereas deployed systems receive ASR output, we run every comparison with both, using a compact speechLLM (frozen Whisper-medium encoder, 3B LLM) on IEMOCAP and MELD. The classification head improves Macro F1 in 10 of 14 configurations. On IEMOCAP, it improves every configuration using ASR transcripts, reaching 76.97\% Macro F1, with a significant gain when using speech alone. On MELD, where ASR transcripts have a 32.38\% word error rate, it helps with speech alone but not with ASR transcripts. The benefit thus depends on both the dataset and the transcript source: in 4 of the 6 configurations that use text, the head's effect changes sign between ground-truth and ASR transcripts. Conclusions drawn with ground-truth transcripts therefore need not hold with ASR transcripts. Finally, comparing the learned class vectors with the LLM's vocabulary shows that, on IEMOCAP and MELD, their nearest tokens are mostly emotion-related words rather than explicit emotion labels.
comment: Under review at ACL Rolling Review (ARR)

title: WILSON - Multi-magnification composites as a foundation for patient-level pathology analysis and diagnostic text generation
comments: 61 pages, 6 main figures, with 11 additional figures and 29 tables in the appendices
summary: Pathologists examine tissue sections across multiple magnifications and slides, integrating morphological information to establish a diagnosis. In contrast, most pathology foundation models encode thousands of image patches from a single representative ("best") slide and aggregate their features, limiting multiscale and patient-level contextual integration. Here we introduce WILSON, a vision-language foundation model that represents whole-slide images and multi-slide cases through multi-magnification composites. Trained on approximately 189,000 slides spanning 42 organs and 838 diagnostic entities, WILSON enables patient-level analysis, multimodal retrieval and diagnostic text generation. Without task-specific training, WILSON outperformed a dedicated case-level model (macro-F1, 0.52 versus 0.38) and matched substantially larger slide-level models while requiring 400-1,350 times fewer computational operations. End-to-end fine-tuning improved breast cancer subtyping and stromal lymphocyte grading. WILSON also surpassed PRISM in image-text retrieval (recall@1, 75.6% versus 58.1%) and generated diagnostic descriptions that received higher ratings from five board-certified pathologists than competing models. These findings demonstrate that compact, multiscale representations can support computationally efficient, clinically grounded pathology foundation models.
comment: 61 pages, 6 main figures, with 11 additional figures and 29 tables in the appendices

title: Real-Time Adaptive Filtering and the Boxcar Limit in Superconducting Qubit Readout
summary: Control and readout systems for superconducting quantum computing support real-time control and high-fidelity qubit-state discrimination. We examine when additional digital processing improves readout fidelity. A common baseline for dispersive readout uses a boxcar averager to compute a uniformly weighted average over a fixed window followed by threshold-based state assignment. We evaluated an adaptive finite-impulse-response (FIR) filter trained in real time using the least-mean-squares (LMS) algorithm on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) quantum controller. We also analyzed measured readout shots offline to compare the frozen filter with boxcar averaging, and evaluate per-sample weighting plus sequential detection. For the fixed FIR filters tested, summing the filtered samples gives the boxcar sum multiplied by one complex number apart from a small edge correction. We call this the kernel collapse. The multiplication scales the state separation and noise equally without improving state discrimination, and we call this the boxcar limit. The frozen LMS filter reduces trace noise, but shows no resolved improvement in readout fidelity. On a 2D transmon, optimizing the readout window accounted for much of the improvement over full-window integration. We then examined how changing the decision method could reduce calibration effort and decision time. On a higher-fidelity 3D ancilla readout, our modeled template estimation reached the same fidelity target as direct averaging with 89.8% fewer labeled shots per state. Offline sequential replay assigned most shots before the acquisition window ended. These results distinguish waveform denoising from state-discrimination improvement, and motivate direct control of decision weights and assignment time in dispersive readout.

title: RDSE: Real-Time Directional Speech Enhancement Framework for Dual-Mic Commodity Smartphones
comments: Accepted at IEEE IECON 2026 (17 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables). Project page: https://danish-research.github.io/rdse-research.github.io/
summary: Audio-visual zooming on mobile devices is fundamentally constrained by limited microphone count, compute resource, unknown array geometry, and weak assumptions on real-world acoustic conditions. We present RDSE: Real-Time Directional Speech Enhancement Framework, a hybrid pipeline that combines traditional signal processing and modern machine learning methods for dual-microphone low-end smartphones. Unlike tightly coupled AV systems that continuously use visual feeds or embeddings, RDSE decouples visual interaction from feature inference, using camera input solely to parameterize the steering vector for spatial filtering. The proposed system uses four modules: dereverberation network, a beamformer with a temporal convolutional network, and a MetricGAN based denoiser. Extensive evaluation on benchmark data and real-world recordings demonstrates effective zooming without precise geometry calibration. Comparative experiments show competitive performance to existing methods. Proposed system is rigorously tested for statistical validity, ablation study, latency profiling, and practicality through real-time live-streaming.
comment: Accepted at IEEE IECON 2026 (17 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables). Project page: https://danish-research.github.io/rdse-research.github.io/

title: Universal Distributed Feature Extraction Complementary to Side Information via H-Score
summary: This paper considers a distributed estimation system where edge nodes transmit averaged features to a center node for parameter estimation. A key challenge arises when the center node possesses auxiliary side information: how to design local extractors that are universally optimal for any downstream task, while avoiding redundancy with the side information. To tackle this problem, we orthogonally decompose the joint function space and demonstrate in the weak-dependence regime that the modal decomposition of the canonical dependence kernel's conditional-additive component yields optimal, task-independent features. We construct a distributed nested H-score to learn this decomposition and show that, under a limited feature budget, the mean-squared error (MSE) gap to the best task-specific features is determined solely by the task's alignment with the discarded, least informative modes, and vanishes to leading order for every square-integrable task once the budget is sufficient.

title: From Optical Flow to Safety: Visual Safety Certification via Scale-Free Relative Motion
summary: Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification, without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C$^3$BF). An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in $98.3\%$ of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in $93$ of $100$ real-world trials.

title: The role of distributed friction dynamics on heave-induced motion of offshore drilling systems: modelling, analysis, and simulations
summary: This paper investigates the influence of friction dynamics on heave-induced disturbance propagation using a coupled hydraulic-structural drilling model formulated as a semilinear interconnection of ordinary and hyperbolic partial differential equations (ODE-PDEs), and capturing spatially distributed memory effects in the drillstring-wellbore interaction. First, local and global existence and uniqueness results are established, and sufficient conditions for boundedness and input-to-state stability are deduced via a small-gain analysis. Subsequently, extensive numerical investigations are carried out, including harmonic excitation studies, nonlinear distortion analysis, spatial amplification investigations, mechanism-isolation experiments, parameter sensitivity analysis, and broadband simulations under realistic offshore sea-state excitation. The simulation results indicate that, whilst the hydraulic response is governed primarily by wave propagation phenomena, compressibility, and boundary reflections, the structural dynamics display substantially greater sensitivity to distributed friction effects. Furthermore, drillstring-wellbore friction is shown to have a relatively limited influence on well-posedness but a potentially significant impact on stability margins. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for coupled hydraulic-structural dynamics and distributed friction mechanisms when analysing, monitoring, and controlling offshore drilling systems.

title: Galerkin Approximation of the Fractional Sobolev Constant
summary: We establish sharp estimates for the discrete optimal constant of the fractional Sobolev inequality in dimension $N\geq 1$, with fractional exponent $s\in (0,\min\{1,N/2\})$. The convergence rates that we establish take place for the Galerkin approximation with piecewise linear elements, when the problem is posed in the unit ball, for which we employ a quasi-uniform and regular mesh. Since the infimum defining the fractional Sobolev constant is not attained on bounded domains, these estimates quantify how far a piecewise affine mesh of size $h$ can resolve the concentration of the optimizers: the discrete minimizers are close to bubbles concentrated at the scale $h^{2(2-s)/(N+4(1-s))}$, and the energy gap is exactly of order $h^{2(2-s)(N-2s)/(N+4(1-s))}$.

title: Motion-Enabled Tomography of Gaussian-Mixture Particles under Unknown Rigid-Body Motion with Parabolic Trajectories
comments: Submitted to SIAM SIIMS. 38 pages, Noisy 2D reconstruction included
summary: Reconstructing objects with unknown position and/or orientation arises in applications spanning geology to cryo-ET. When the relative motion between the object and the sensing apparatus provides sufficient angular coverage, computerized tomography offers a powerful means of reconstruction. For such scenarios, we propose a parametric spatiotemporal model applied to Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), in which each constituent Gaussian is parameterized by its own angular velocity, parabolic trajectory, and morphology. GMM are a suitable means of reconstruction because they (i) admit accurate approximations in object space and (ii) have a closed form expression under the ray transform; enabling efficient forward predictions and analysis in data space. By decoupling the projectile motion from the rotation and morphology, the full optimization problem can be reduced to two lower-dimensional sub-problems that are easier to optimize. The corresponding algorithm --- which is applicable to objects in Euclidean space of arbitrary dimension --- is validated on an extensive set of noisy 2D simulations. Its performance provides promise for further experimentation in more complex scenarios, such as higher dimensions, objects with deformable body mechanics, and on physical datasets.
comment: Submitted to SIAM SIIMS. 38 pages, Noisy 2D reconstruction included

title: Computing statistical solutions of a Mach 2000 astrophysical jet
summary: The multi-dimensional compressible Euler equations admit non-unique entropy solutions in turbulent regimes, and extreme-Mach astrophysical flows are a natural setting in which this breakdown of deterministic well-posedness becomes computationally visible. We compute statistical solutions of a Mach~2000 astrophysical jet, defined as the pushforward of an initial probability measure through a vectorial lattice Boltzmann method, by Monte Carlo sampling with $M=1000$ realizations on grids of up to $12.8$ million cells. Under mesh refinement the individual realizations diverge pathwise, while the statistical solution converges: Wasserstein distances of the one- and two-point marginals, the ensemble mean, and the ensemble standard deviation all exhibit stable positive convergence rates. A spatially resolved analysis along the jet axis traces this dichotomy to the structure of the one-point laws, which are numerically Dirac in the undisturbed core, skewed in the sheared turbulent regions, and intermittent two-state mixtures at the random leading front. We conclude that the computed statistical solution is non-Dirac and remains stable in the extreme compressible regime, in which no strong solution is expected to exist.

title: Bridging Scales: Asymptotic Analysis and AI-Assisted Formalization
summary: Asymptotic analysis is one of the classical tools for bridging models across scales. Behind many such derivations lies a common symbolic structure: an ansatz, a substitution, an order-by-order matching procedure, and the extraction of effective equations or interface conditions. This article revisits that structure through two representative bridges: the kinetic-to-fluid limit, illustrated by radiative transfer with interface layers and by neural-network approximations of Boltzmann equations, and the quantum-to-classical limit, illustrated by the Frozen Gaussian Approximation and its Dirac extension. We then explain why such derivations are natural candidates for AI-assisted formalization: their recurring symbolic structures can be organized, verified, and reused. In this sense, a carefully structured expository paper may serve not only as a review, but also as a mathematical seed for future AI-assisted environments.

title: Bregman-projected mirror methods for regularized stationary mean-field games
summary: We develop and analyze a Bregman-projected mirror iteration for low-order regularizations of stationary mean-field game (MFG) systems in their natural Banach space setting. For separable Hamiltonians of the form $H(x,p,m)=H_0(x,p)-g(m)$, with quadratic or super-quadratic Hamiltonian growth and linear or super-linear density couplings, we formulate a low-order $\barγ$-Laplacian regularization of the stationary MFG system as a variational inequality on $L^{\barβ}(\mathbb T^d)\times W^{1,\barγ}(\mathbb T^d)$. To approximate solutions of this regularized variational inequality, we introduce a Bregman geometry matched to the mixed Lebesgue-Sobolev exponents of the problem and analyze the exact constrained one-step mirror iteration and a frozen two-step variant. Under quantitative monotonicity of the coupling, both exact iterations converge strongly to the unique solution of the regularized variational inequality for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, under natural summability conditions on the step sizes. Along weakly convergent vanishing-regularization sequences, we also prove strong convergence in the full product space. Numerical experiments in one and two dimensions show first-order accuracy on manufactured solutions and weak dependence of outer iteration counts on the tested grids. At matched effective step sizes, the frozen two-step and one-step implementations agree up to inner-solve accuracy, while the latter requires fewer mirror solves.

title: A multilevel stochastic-gradient neural solver for boundary integral equations
summary: We propose a multilevel stochastic-gradient neural solver (MLSG) for second-kind boundary integral equations. MLSG represents the unknown boundary density using a neural network optimized by stochastic residual minimization over a hierarchy of successively refined Nyström discretizations. Upon transitioning from one level to the next, the network parameters obtained on the previous level initialize training on the current one. This coarse-to-fine strategy retains a continuous, grid-independent density representation and is designed to reduce the total computational effort required to reach a prescribed residual tolerance at the target resolution. The algorithm avoids grid-transfer operators and hierarchical fast-summation machinery, relying instead on batched kernel evaluations and standard network forward and backward passes that map efficiently onto modern GPU architectures. For uniformly stable second-kind discretizations, so strongly nonuniform contraction rates originate in the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) rather than in the discretized operator. Within each level, parameter updates can reshape the NTK, while refinement re-samples the tangent kernel on a richer discrete space and reveals directions that were not adequately resolved on coarser levels. A cross-level estimate bounds the warm-start loss in terms of the preceding training tolerance and quadrature error, motivating a tolerance schedule that balances optimization and discretization errors. Experiments on Laplace/Poisson and Helmholtz problems in two and three dimensions, together with an exterior Robin problem on a hypersurface in $\R^4$, demonstrate the method under both parametric and signed-distance surface representations at up to million-scale discretizations.

title: Structure-Preserving Reduced-Order Modeling via Low-Rank Transport Signatures
summary: Parametrized PDEs with density-valued solutions are often difficult to approximate with classical linear reduced-order models, especially in transport-dominated regimes. We introduce an optimal-transport-based reduced-order modeling that represents each density by the Kantorovich potential transporting a fixed reference density to the target density, and then maps these potentials to transport signatures using a weighted Laplacian associated with the reference measure. This embeds the density-valued solution map in a Hilbert space while preserving control of the induced transport maps and Wasserstein error. We treat the signature map as a continuous matrix indexed by parameters and space, construct a low-rank skeleton decomposition using a maximal-volume criterion, and learn the parameter-to-coefficient map with a neural network for efficient non-intrusive online evaluation. The reconstructed solution is obtained by pushing forward the reference density, so mass and positivity preservation is built into the method. We prove a mean-squared Wasserstein error bound separating low-rank approximation, discretization, sampling, and learning errors, and demonstrate the method on density-valued continuity equation and Burgers equation, where transport signatures yield substantially lower-rank structure than the original density snapshots.

title: Deep Stochastic Residual Methods for Fully Nonlinear Parabolic Equations
summary: We develop and analyze neural stochastic residual methods for fully nonlinear parabolic terminal problems under exact diffusion sampling. A quadratic stochastic residual supports global training and backward regression with scalar networks and losses involving only spatial derivatives. For global training, the correction removes a Hessian penalty from the limiting first-order loss. Under a uniform output regularity budget, we bound the continuous residual norm by the square roots of the global loss or normalized backward-regression excess loss, an $O(h^{1/2})$ discretization term for time step $h$, and terminal error. Residual stability then gives value, gradient and Hessian error bounds. Under suitable solution and terminal assumptions, we construct admissible networks with $O(h^{1/2})$ bounds on these approximation errors and the square roots of both loss criteria. In ten-dimensional backward-regression tests using a shared schedule tuned for the quadratic residual, mean relative Hessian errors are $5$--$6\%$ with the quadratic residual and about $15\%$ with the first-order residual. Tuned backward regression achieves Hessian accuracy comparable to physics-informed neural networks across the tested nonlinear coefficients. Translation tests show that the ratio of Hessian error to residual can grow sharply under a fixed sampling law.

title: A stable and efficient Galerkin spectral method with asymmetrically-weighted Hermite functions for the Vlasov-Poisson system
summary: We analyze a Galerkin spectral method applied to the Vlasov-Poisson (VP) system based on time-independent asymmetrically-weighted (AW) Hermite functions in velocity. The VP system is written as an hyperbolic system using AW Hermite functions in velocity. Unlike the classical Petrov-Galerkin spectral method, which is not stable, the proposed Galerkin spectral method admits a natural stability in the unweighted L2 norm. This stability property enables a rigorous convergence analysis of the method. For sufficiently regular solutions with exponential decay in velocity, we establish error estimates between the exact and numerical solutions and prove convergence of the Galerkin spectral method. In particular, the method achieves spectral convergence in Sobolev spaces, with convergence rates determined by the regularity of the exact solution. Since the Gram matrix arising from the proposed Galerkin method is dense, we derive an equivalent form that retains the same approximation properties while preserving the sparsity structure similar to the classical Petrov-Galerkin method.

title: Advanced Linear Algebra with Applications - Part I (Numerical linear algebra for PDEs, machine learning, and data assimilation)
comments: 101 pages, 24 figures. Lecture notes; Part I of a two-part master's course. Generative AI (Claude Opus 5, Anthropic) was used to help identify seminal references, improve the language, and improve the graphical content; all statements, proofs, and references have been checked by the authors, who take full responsibility for the contents. Code: https://github.com/vicdolean/scicomp_examples
summary: These lecture notes form the first part of a master's-level course on advanced numerical linear algebra. Their aim is not only to present the classical algorithms, but to show why the subject has become considerably more central than it was a generation ago. Numerical linear algebra grew up alongside the numerical solution of partial differential equations, and for a long time that is where its large sparse systems came from. Ranking the nodes of a network, assimilating observations into a weather forecast, and fitting a model to a large noisy data set now lead to problems of the same kind: too large to factorise, structured, and accessible only through matrix-vector products. Strikingly few ideas are needed for all of them. Each chapter therefore develops a standard topic and then puts it to work outside its original setting. We treat norms, factorisations, conditioning and floating-point arithmetic; sparse matrices arising from finite differences, from graphs and from machine learning; stationary iterations and the smoothing property; the conjugate gradient and Lanczos methods, with spectral clustering and regularisation by early stopping; Arnoldi and GMRES, with PageRank and large least squares; and finally preconditioning, Schwarz domain decomposition and multigrid. We assume a first course in linear algebra. Every section closes with a summary of what should be retained and every chapter with exercises, several drawn from past examinations. Accompanying Python code reproduces the numerical illustrations.
comment: 101 pages, 24 figures. Lecture notes; Part I of a two-part master's course. Generative AI (Claude Opus 5, Anthropic) was used to help identify seminal references, improve the language, and improve the graphical content; all statements, proofs, and references have been checked by the authors, who take full responsibility for the contents. Code: https://github.com/vicdolean/scicomp_examples

title: A simple stability analysis of the Lanczos algorithm in finite precision arithmetic
summary: We give a self-contained analysis of the symmetric Lanczos algorithm without reorthogonalization when computations are performed inexactly. We show the computed Lanczos vectors are well-behaved locally. From this we (i) prove Paige's loss-of-orthogonality identity, and (ii) construct a Greenbaum-type backward stability result, exhibiting a nearby problem on which exact Lanczos produces the computed tridiagonal matrix. This allows us to derive several facts about the computed Ritz values at the original eigenvalues. Our analysis simplifies the analyses of Paige and Greenbaum, at the cost of hiding polynomial factors in the iteration count.

title: High-order entropy-stable isothermal wall boundary condition for the compressible Navier--Stokes equations
summary: Entropy-stable boundary conditions are critical for ensuring that the corresponding numerical scheme satisfies the discrete entropy inequality, thus mimicking the second law of thermodynamics for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations discretely. Provably entropy-stable adiabatic wall boundary conditions were introduced in Parsani 2014~\cite{parsani2014entropy}. These discrete wall boundary conditions were further generalized in Dalcin 2019~\cite{dalcin2019conservative} to a moving adiabatic solid wall or a wall with a prescribed heat flux for the compressible Navier--Stokes equations discretized by using summation-by-parts (SBP) and simultaneous-approximation-term (SAT) operators. Currently, no entropy-stable formulation using SBP-SAT operators for isothermal wall boundary conditions is available in the literature. This paper presents new isothermal no-slip wall boundary conditions that: 1) enforce the $T|_{y=0}=T^{wall}$ and $\vec{v}|_{y=0}=\vec{v}^{wall}$ conditions with the design order of accuracy while maintaining stability, 2) provide the correct sign of entropy production at the wall, and 3) mimic the entropy balance of the Navier-Stokes equations at the discrete level. The structure-preserving and design-order properties of the proposed methodology are demonstrated and verified on standard benchmark problems for compressible flows.

title: A Coupled Fluid Naghdi Shell Windkessel Model for Pulmonary Artery Banding: Partitioned Numerical Scheme and Parameter Estimation
summary:
We develop a 3D fluid structure interaction model for blood flow through deformable vessels with localized constrictions, motivated by pulmonary artery banding in neonates with congenital heart disease. The model couples incompressible Navier Stokes equations in an Arbitrary Lagrangian Eulerian framework with a Naghdi shell model for the arterial wall and a three element Windkessel model for downstream circulation. The shell describes a 3D cylindrical vessel wall with variable radius and is defined on a 2D reference domain. Its low regularity formulation retains membrane, bending, and transverse shear deformation while requiring only first derivatives of the reference midsurface, accommodating piecewise smooth geometries with discontinuous surface slopes.
  We derive the coupled variational formulation and develop a non-iterative partitioned scheme with a Robin-type interface condition incorporating arterial wall inertia. For a linearized fixed domain problem, we establish a discrete energy estimate under suitable assumptions. A unscented Kalman filter estimates proximal and distal resistances and compliance from inlet-pressure observations. Numerical experiments demonstrate consistent pressure wave propagation and wall deformation under spatial and temporal refinement. Comparisons of the standard Naghdi shell and a modified, predominantly radial shell model reveal how structural deformation mechanisms affect wave speed and displacement. An idealized pulmonary artery banding example demonstrates the coupled fluid shell Windkessel model with parameter estimation. The framework enables investigation of the hemodynamic and mechanical effects of localized constrictions and their dependence on downstream vascular properties.

title: A Mixed Elliptic--Hyperbolic Monge--Ampère Problem: Modeling and a Least-Squares Solver
comments: 26 pages, 10 figures, submitted to SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing
summary: We consider a transport problem motivated by freeform optical design of a parallel-to-far-field reflector. Classical formulations rely on either elliptic or hyperbolic Monge--Ampère equations, leading to globally convex/concave or saddle-shape reflector geometries, respectively. However, the design of smooth reflector arrays may require optical surfaces combining both types of curvature. To address this, we introduce a mixed elliptic--hyperbolic Monge--Ampère system obtained by partitioning the source domain into one elliptic and one hyperbolic subregion, and we develop a least-squares method for its numerical approximation. Numerical examples demonstrate the ability of the proposed framework to compute both isolated and periodic mixed-type transport solutions, yielding smooth reflector configurations.
comment: 26 pages, 10 figures, submitted to SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing

title: Toward Spectral Deferred Correction Methods for Stochastic Differential Equations
summary: The numerical solution of stochastic differential equations is computationally very demanding. Often it is of interest to evaluate certain moments, e.g., the expectation, by Monte Carlo sampling, thus requiring the computation of numerous realizations. The discretization error of the numerical scheme induces bias in the computed Monte Carlo estimator. As popular numerical schemes, like Euler-Maruyama or Milstein, are low-order, even reasonably coarse error bounds for the simulation are costly to achieve. While the evaluation of moments requires only weak convergence, in other applications like parameter estimation, strong convergence is important, but higher-order is typically harder to obtain in the strong than in the weak sense. In this paper we develop an efficient method with the potential of achieving higher strong and weak convergence order. It is based on the smooth approximation of Brownian bridges combined with spectral deferred correction methods well known for the numerical solution of ordinary differential equations. We discuss convergence, and present numerical results.

title: Interacting Annealed Importance Sampling via Population-Based MCMC Kernels
comments: 34 pages, 14 figures (Accepted by SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing)
summary: Sampling from a multimodal distribution is a fundamental and challenging problem in computational science and statistics. Among various approaches proposed for this task, one popular method is Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS). In this paper, we propose an interaction-based version of AIS by combining it with population-based Monte Carlo methods to improve its efficiency. By keeping track of an ensemble instead of a single sampler along some continuation path between the starting distribution and the target distribution, we take advantage of the interaction within the ensemble to encourage the exploration of undiscovered modes. Specifically, our main idea is to utilize either the snooker algorithm or the genetic algorithm used in Evolutionary Monte Carlo. We discuss how the proposed algorithm can be implemented and derive a partial differential equation governing the evolution of the ensemble under the continuous time and mean-field limit. We also test the efficiency of the proposed algorithm on various continuous and discrete distributions.
comment: 34 pages, 14 figures (Accepted by SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing)

title: A Level Set Method on Particle Flow Maps
summary: Accurate interface tracking is central to numerical simulations involving moving boundaries, including multiphase flows, free-surface dynamics, phase-change problems, and other interface-driven processes in computational mechanics. Although level set methods provide a flexible implicit representation of evolving interfaces, their grid-based advection and reinitialization procedures often introduce numerical diffusion, volume loss, and degradation of thin or highly curved structures. This paper introduces a Particle Flow Map Level Set (PFM-LS) method that addresses these limitations by transporting interface geometry through particle-carried bidirectional flow maps. In contrast to particle level set methods that use particles mainly as corrective markers, PFM-LS uses particles as primary carriers of level-set values, gradients, and Hessians within a narrow band around the interface. The method combines long-range flow-map transport, high-order particle-grid reconstruction, adaptive particle control, and a hybrid particle-grid redistancing scheme to preserve both signed-distance consistency and sub-grid geometric features. Numerical benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including topology-change tests, chamfer and Hausdorff shape-error metrics, and coupling to an incompressible free-surface flow solver, show that PFM-LS achieves strong volume preservation, high shape fidelity, and near fourth-order convergence, outperforming a broad range of existing level set and reference-map-based methods.

title: Rate-induced tipping in a solvable model with the Allee effect
summary: We present a novel exactly solvable ordinary differential equation model for rate-induced tipping: a dynamic phenomenon of dynamical systems where a time-dependent parameter triggers the transition of stability of a system. Our model contains an Allee effect that induces a saddle point and admits an explicit solution along with the extinction threshold of a time-dependent Allee parameter. More specifically, we derive an integral inequality that serves as a necessary condition for the occurrence of rate-induced tipping. A remarkable point in the proposed model is that it can handle population extinction such that the solution completely vanishes in a finite amount of time. An unconditionally stable cubature method suitable for our model is proposed, and its superiority over the classical forward Euler method is discussed. As a proof of concept, the model reproduces the rise and fall of the membership of inland fisheries cooperatives in Japan from 1963 to 2023. The proposed model serves as a tractable tool for studying R-tipping phenomena.

title: Structural conditions on trust-region radius updates. Part I: first-order convergence and complexity
summary:
Trust-region methods differ chiefly in how they update the radius, and each rule has traditionally been analysed on its own terms. We show that three structural conditions on the radius sequence suffice: a lower bound relative to the gradient norm, a contraction on unsuccessful iterations, and a controlled expansion on successful ones. A mechanism is weakly admissible if it satisfies the first two, and strongly admissible if it satisfies the first and third.
  Strong admissibility yields the optimal worst-case complexity $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ for first-order stationarity, and extends global convergence to model Hessians growing linearly with the iteration; weak admissibility gives $\lim_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\| = 0$ under uniformly bounded model Hessians. Both hold for every rule in the class, so a new mechanism is covered by verifying two inequalities rather than by a fresh convergence proof.
  We verify admissibility for five mechanism classes (fixed-factor, step-driven, retrospective, criticality-anchored and gradient-scaled), prove convergence of the retrospective update under linearly growing model Hessians, and extend the Lyapunov framework of Curtis and Scheinberg (2020), Wang and Yuan (2022) to three distinct scaling factors with decoupled step acceptance, covering $η= 0$; its stochastic version specialises to the deterministic gradient-scaled rule.
  Part II treats the asymptotic behaviour of the radius and convergence to second-order critical points.

title: Microstructure-Conditioned Surrogate Models for Graded Multiscale Optimization of Mycelium Composites
summary: Emerging sustainable materials increasingly rely on engineered hierarchy and microstructure to achieve control of their properties and mechanical behavior. Optimizing these materials with controllable microstructures requires efficient multiscale simulations. Data-driven surrogate models for the microscale can accelerate multiscale simulations, but require large amounts of data even for a fixed microstructure. When a range of microstructures is considered, as is the case in multiscale optimization, even more data is needed to train a surrogate. To overcome this challenge, we condition a hybrid physics-data surrogate on microstructural variables using a hypernetwork. This approach enables accurate predictions of multiscale mechanical behavior for a mycelium-woodchip composite material, even when trained on small datasets. The conditioned surrogate makes multiscale simulations of functionally graded structures tractable, and we validate it against a full FE^2 simulation. We optimize a graded multiscale disk, and reduce the peak stress by 43% compared to one with a random microstructure. Then, we go one step further, conditioning the network directly on manufacturing variables that can have a complex influence on the microstructure. This is a practical route to engineer the microscale for desired macroscale behavior. This contribution highlights the benefits of microarchitectured structures and demonstrates how conditioned surrogate models enable their multiscale optimization, which will accelerate the development and design of future sustainable materials and structures.

title: A counterexample to Kenig's conjecture for the Laplace double-layer operator
summary: We disprove Kenig's 1994 spectral-radius conjecture for the double-layer operator in every dimension $d\ge2$. For every $t>1/2$ sufficiently close to $1/2$, we construct a bounded simply connected Lipschitz domain with connected boundary such that the double-layer operator on $L^2$ with respect to the surface measure has $\pm \mathrm{i} t$ in its Fredholm essential spectrum. In particular, the essential spectral radius is greater than $1/2$. In the plane, the boundary may be chosen differentiable everywhere and smooth away from a single point. Our planar construction develops a refinement mechanism that produces unbounded growth of adjoint resolvent solutions with fixed forcing while keeping the graph slopes uniformly bounded. A closed recursion for the density and its image under an auxiliary singular integral reduces the growth estimate to a certified inequality for Hermitian $2\times2$ matrices. The certificate uses continuous estimates, exact rational arithmetic and rigorous interval enclosures. Localisation and rescaled graph insertions then produce a weakly null sequence of normalised approximate eigenvectors for the adjoint double-layer operator on one bounded boundary. A compact intertwining relation on Cartesian products of the planar domain with cubes gives the higher-dimensional examples without changing the spectral parameter.

title: Computational Taxonomy for visualizing and exploring systems with functional response dynamics: soybean's O2-respiration example
summary: A collective of 1684 O2-respiration curves of 183 dimensions are collected along soybeans' germinating process with 72 covariate feature-measurements. We develop a computational thematic platform for first discovering and exposing heterogeneous typical-shapes and then extracting readable, visible and explainable pattern information with biological implications when comparing between them. Via existing knowledge on seeds of much smaller sizes, such collective of O2-respiration curves are expected to generally embrace the two-stage or sigmoidal patterns. However, due to Soybean's relatively large surface area with harder to control and retain experimental conditions, much diverse and heterogeneous shapes are highly expected. Shannon entropy is applied to capture potential categorical nature across the 183 time-points, while scaled mutual information is used to evaluate pattern-consistency. Three motifs are determined to partition the temporal time-points into three regions: W1 on [1, 20], W2 on [21, 60] and W3 on [61, 183]. Each curve is partitioned into three segments accordingly. Hierarchical cluster algorithm is applied onto these motif-region-specific curve-segments, respectively. Five clusters of shapes on W1 are selected, four on W2 and four on W3. We computationally build a tree-geometry-based Taxonomic Hierarchy to organize these 80 curve-shapes into 15 typical shapes. Then we compare among these typical shapes to extract and display their differences through block-sustained heatmaps. Each focal block is expressed va a network of covariate features to reveal dominant interacting effects of various orders. Scientific explanations and understanding are to be rested on the collected heatmaps and coupled networks collectively.

title: Local Manifold Attention for Recovery and Generation of Rare 3D Human Poses
summary: A rare 3D human pose in a motion sequence may reflect either a genuine movement or an estimation error, making correction difficult when reference databases contain few comparable examples. We investigate whether local geometric structure can support the recovery and generation of rare configura- tions, using motion-capture sequences from AMASS, which unifies datasets through a common parametric human-body model, together with video-based pose estimates. We develop the cylindrical manifold attention transformer (CMAT), which extends local manifold fitting through geometry- and task- dependent neighborhood weights. For motion correction, Self-Action CMAT draws on comparable windows within a sequence, adjusts their contributions for neighborhood imbalance and temporal dependence, and integrates local geometry with robust temporal regularization. Experiments on perturbed and estimated motions show reductions in position and acceleration errors, with component analyses examining how weighting and temporal processing con- tribute to recovery. The controlled correction comparisons are exploratory and conditional on the selected motion-amplitude bound. For generation, Rarity-preserving CMAT explores locally supported configurations subject to independently calibrated rarity and separation from stored observations. Under common screening criteria, it achieves a higher yield of eligible rare poses than the evaluated generation baselines.

title: Logistic vegetation trajectories and their implications for land surface phenology
summary: Vegetation trajectories describe canopy development and underpin phenological metrics, including the start and end of the growing season. We derive a generalized logistic function (GLF) to represent canopy growth under explicit assumptions: exponential development combined with a Michaelis-Menten-type saturating response yields an ordinary logistic function, and a power transformation introduces asymmetry. Using the GLF as a common mathematical basis, we relate trajectory shape to phenological metrics and date uncertainty. We derive shape-dependent relative thresholds for derivative-defined transition points and recover the 9.18% onset threshold for an isolated ordinary logistic growth curve under the small-slope approximation. For a symmetric double-logistic seasonal trajectory, we derive the realized amplitude, full width at half maximum and a critical dimensionless temporal separation between growth and senescence components at which interior third-derivative extrema merge. Exact curvature-change transition points also depend on the metric assigned to the time and response axes. Local noise propagation and 4,800 nonlinear fits show how trajectory geometry affects date uncertainty: additional shape flexibility can reduce bias while increasing uncertainty in the seasonal tails. Together, these results explain how trajectory shape determines the location and existence of phenological transition points and uncertainty in their estimated dates. The framework supports phenology retrieval that preserves the underlying trajectory and interprets each metric through its mathematical definition and uncertainty.

title: State Space Modeling of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process with Measurement Error: An Application to Microbiome Data
summary:
Understanding the temporal dynamics of the human microbiome is critical for deciphering host-microbe interactions and identifying responses to environmental or physiological disruptions. In this study, we develop a likelihood-based framework grounded in Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) state-space modeling to analyze longitudinal microbiome data. By applying log-ratio transformations to genus-level relative abundances, we accommodate the compositional nature of microbiome profiles and enable biologically interpretable inference.
  We estimate the mean reversion rate of the OU process using maximum likelihood estimation and construct profile likelihood confidence intervals to assess temporal stability. Biologically, higher estimated mean-reversion rates correspond to stronger regulatory feedback and thus greater temporal stability of the gut microbiome, whereas lower rates reflect weaker stabilization and slower recovery from perturbations. In the datasets analyzed here, most estimated mean reversion rates were between 0.12 and 0.36, corresponding to a half-life in the range 2-6 days for the system to return to the equilibrium level. These mean-reversion rates are substantially lower than previous estimates obtained from OU models that did not account for measurement error. To capture structural shifts in microbial dynamics, we propose a statistical testing procedure that compares a single-parameter model to a split-parameter model across disrupted time periods. We also propose an OUSSM to jointly model multiple microbes, taking into account the special measurement error covariance structure for log-ratio transformed data.

title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data
summary: Neuroimaging analysis commonly involves classifying cognitive conditions, identifying task-relevant brain regions, and examining functional connectivity. These objectives are typically addressed separately, without a model-based framework. In contrast, we propose a Bayesian distance-weighted Ising model that integrates classification, regional importance, and connectivity analysis. The model captures dependence among task labels based on connectivities between functional signals, while region-of-interest (ROI)-specific interaction parameters account for spatial heterogeneity and quantify regional contributions to task discrimination. However, inference is challenging because the signals may be observed on unequal time grids and the likelihood function contains an intractable normalising constant. To address this, we use a basis expansion and an auxiliary variable Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply the method to functional near-infrared spectroscopy data from younger and older adults, comparing resting-state and task-related activity. The model achieves high classification accuracy and reveals age-dependent patterns of regional importance and connectivity. Among younger adults, the left orbitofrontal cortex contributes more strongly to task discrimination than the dorsolateral prefrontal and frontopolar cortices, whereas regional differences are less evident among older adults. Older adults also exhibit greater bilateral connectivity between corresponding ROIs, consistent with reduced hemispheric lateralisation.

title: A multivariate index for estimating seasonal shifts from temperature curves
comments: 30 pages, 11 numbered figures, 1 table, and a graphical abstract. Revised manuscript under review at Earth Systems and Environment
summary: Seasonal timing is often studied using fixed calendar seasons, temperature thresholds, or a fixed smoothing parameter applied across all years. These may be sensitive to changes in variability over time. To address this, we propose the Seasonal Adaptive LocalisabLe Index (SALLI), a multivariate index, for characterising seasonality from daily temperature curves observed over complete seasons. SALLI uses Significant Zero Crossings of Derivatives (SiZer) to identify significant increases and decreases across a range of smoothing levels. It uses this information to select a smoothing level for each year. The method assumes one main warm peak and one cool trough per annual cycle. For each year, SALLI estimates the annual temperature curve and the midpoints of the four seasons and temperatures. These estimates describe changes in both seasonal timing and temperature. We illustrate SALLI using Australian maximum temperature data from 1965 to 2024. Comparisons of SALLI estimates over the first and last decades show not only a warming, but a shift to earlier seasons, with the midpoints of spring, summer, and winter occurring roughly a week earlier. All four seasonal midpoints become warmer, with the largest increases occurring in summer (1.37 $^\circ$C) and spring (1.22 $^\circ$C). Warming is evident across time, whereas the clearest shift in seasonal timing emerges after the 2000s. By estimating both timing and temperature at each seasonal midpoint, SALLI locates where changes occur on the annual temperature curve, providing information that is more robust and data-driven than fixed thresholds, fixed calendar seasons, or a single smoothing choice.

title: Financial Literacy and the Functional Shape of Subjective Time Deformation in Intertemporal Choice
comments: 31 pages, 11 figures (4 in main text, 7 in appendices)
summary: Intertemporal decisions are commonly summarized by a single discount parameter, although individuals with similar overall discounting intensity may value short-, medium-, and long-term delays differently. This study investigates whether financial literacy is associated with these horizon-specific differences by treating reconstructed subjective time as a functional rather than scalar outcome. Data were collected through a multilingual online questionnaire administered to a convenience and snowball sample of 140 adults, who provided hypothetical equivalence judgments for a future reward of EUR 100 over 13 horizons from 7 days to 5 years, a three-item financial-literacy measure, and measures of temporal perception. Individual discount trajectories were reconstructed and analyzed with function-on-scalar regression, allowing the association with financial literacy to vary across the temporal domain. Because the normalized subjective-time trajectory is not identifiable for flat or reconstruction-degenerate discount profiles, the primary functional analysis included 59 participants, while complementary analyses used the full analytical sample. The primary model provided no evidence of a robust linear association between financial literacy and subjective-time deformation. An exploratory categorical specification indicated heterogeneity across financial-literacy levels and departure from a linear-score representation, although individual contrasts were imprecise and sensitive to specification. The relationship between financial literacy and intertemporal valuation may thus be more complex than a monotonic score effect, and functional data analytics can reveal horizon-specific structure that scalar summaries obscure. Given the convenience sample and the reduced identified sample, the results are exploratory and require validation in larger independent samples.
comment: 31 pages, 11 figures (4 in main text, 7 in appendices)

title: Quantifying Uncertainty Bounds in Spectral Shallow Water Bathymetry: The Profile Likelihood Framework for Semi-Analytical Models
summary:
Accurate bathymetric mapping in shallow waters is critical for coastal monitoring, navigation safety, and environmental conservation. While semi-analytical (SA) models have proven effective for estimating water column depth (WCD) from optical remote sensing data, quantifying the associated uncertainties remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a unified framework based on profile likelihood to evaluate WCD uncertainties in Semi-Analytical (SA) models, bridging traditional variance-covariance methods with likelihood-based inference. Through controlled simulations, we systematically assess the performance of first-order statistical tests-likelihood ratio, Wald (observed and expected), and score tests-across varying environmental conditions and sensor configurations.

Our results demonstrate that the expected Fisher information Wald test, equivalent to classical variance-covariance propagation, provides reliable uncertainty bounds in hyperspectral settings with clear waters. However, its performance deteriorates in multispectral applications and complex water conditions, where likelihood ratio tests prove more robust. This divergence highlights fundamental limitations in the small-sample regime typical of per-pixel spectral bathymetry. Notably, even under idealized conditions with true parameter initialization, local optimization challenges in SA models can compromise both parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, suggesting even greater challenges in practical applications with less favorable initialization. The findings underscore the importance of robust statistical inference in improving the reliability of bathymetric products for operational applications.

title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials
summary: Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material's internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions. This term is governed by two latent physical processes, a molar-mass surface and a Debye-temperature curve, neither of which is observed directly. Instead, both must be recovered from internal energy and pressure, which are derivatives of the free energy, subject to thermodynamic constraints. Existing EOS tables are typically built through material-specific hand-tuning, a process that is tedious, does not scale across materials or conditions, and offers no guarantee of thermodynamic consistency. We propose a partitioned statistical framework that infers molar mass and Debye temperature directly from EOS data, guaranteeing thermodynamic consistency by construction. Local molar-mass behavior is captured with polynomial basis functions across domain partitions, while the Debye temperature is modeled with an I-spline basis. In simulations and a carbon dioxide case study, the method accurately recovers the underlying physical quantities, improves prediction of held-out energy and pressure data, and provides uncertainty quantification while scaling with EOS table size.

title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes
comments: 45 pages, 2 figures. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23262505. v2 consolidates the work into a single document at the moderators' request. v1 was the theoretical part only; v2 adds the diagnostics, an application to a published credit-scoring study, and an impossibility result for selective labeling. Parts are under review separately as two papers
summary: When an outcome is missing not at random, identification is commonly restored by a shadow variable: a covariate that predicts the outcome but is excluded from the response mechanism. The literature treats the first requirement, relevance, as a yes-or-no condition. We make it continuous, parametrizing it by a scalar that scales the shadow variable's entire contribution to the moment conditions, and ask what inference costs as that scalar vanishes. One functional of the inverse weight governs the answer. We characterize it exactly, show that it fixes the effective sample size, and use it to sharpen the rates of the estimator that avoids the weight. The characterization is concrete. Whether the functional saturates or diverges turns not on boundedness of the outcome but on whether the tilting variable has an atom at its essential supremum: a binary outcome saturates, a uniform one does not. It also bounds how far a scanned set reaches, and that reach grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the sample size, so a thousandfold increase buys one unit of tilt while the set to be scanned widens. A reanalyzed credit-scoring study shows the cost: a characteristic an optimizing selector uses cannot satisfy exclusion.
